full_judgment:
5. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor petitioner, submits that both the Courts below committed an error of law in their decisions occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the pre-emption case on the ground that the transfer was not pre-emptible us the same transfer was a heba-bil-ewaz for non pecuniary consideration (i.e. prayer-mat) by the maternal grand-father in favour of his daughter's sons (opposite party Nos. 1 and 2). Mr. Rabbani further submits that the Courts below misunderstood and misconstrued the provision of law in this respect as contained in clause (c) of sub-section (10) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act inasmuch as the daughter's sons were not relations by consanguinity within three degrees of the transferor. 

 6. Mr. A Y Salehuzzaman, the learned Advocate for the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2, submits, on the other hand, that a prayer-mat is not something of pecuniary consideration. In this connection he relied on the case of Syed Ali Gad and others Vs. Alhaj Sardr and others reported in 20 DLR at page 433 where it has been held that a prayer mat is not a pecuniary consideration and a transfer in exchange for this is not pre-emption. The learned Advocate further submits that according to the provision of section 96 sub-section 10(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act a transfer by Heba-bil-ewaz for any non-pecuniary consideration, such as a prayer-mat as in this case, was excluded from pre-emption and, therefore, there is no error of law in the decisions on the part of the learned Courts below in holding that the present transfer is not pre-emptible. 

 From a look at Schedule I of the Succession Act and a plain reading of clause (c) of section 96 (10) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, it is clear that daughter's sons are outside the three degrees of the consanguinity. Therefore, though the finding by both the lower Courts that a transfer of property in exchange for Heba-bil-ewaz in favour of relatives by consanguinity within three degrees of the donor is protected from pre-emption is correct when the donees are within three degrees of consanguinity, but this finding is not correct when a donee is outside the three degrees of consanguinity as in the present case. Consequently, the finding by the lower appellate Court that "admittedly the transfer is to a relation by consanguinity within 3 degrees of the testator or donor. So as per the provision of clause (c) of sub-section (10) of section 96 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act there cannot be pre-emption in such a case." is apparently wrong as the present donees are admittedly outside the three degrees of consanguinity as per the mode of reckoning provided in section 28 of the Succession Act read with First Schedule thereof. Similarly, the finding of the trial Court that “আর এই হেবাবিল এওয়াজটি যেহেতু নানা তার নাতিদের বরাবরে করেছে অর্থাৎ ৩ ডিগ্রির মধ্যেই। কাজেই প্রিয়েমপশন যোগ্য নয়।” is also wrong. 

 8. The decisions cited by the Court below may be applicable in the given facts and circumstances of those cases. But they are not applicable in the present facts and circumstances of the case. The only decision that appears to be applicable is in the case of Tamizunnessa Vs. Umar Ali reported in PLD 1967 (Dhaka) at page 600. But the lower appellate Court has misunderstood the interpretation of section 26F(1)(c) of Bengal Tenancy Act as given in that case wherein it has been held that transfer by heba in favour of the relations by consanguinity within three degrees by the donors are protected. But in the present case as I have already stated above, donor's daughter's two sons (opposite party Nos. 1 and 2) are not relations by consanguinity within three degrees of the donor (late Mir Abdul Jalil) and, therefore, they cannot get the protection of the provision of clause (c) of sub-section (10) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the case referred to above it was held that a nephew is in the three degrees of consanguinity and a transfer by heba to him is protected by clause (c) of section 26F(I); but Reba in favour of first cousin is not protected he being in four degrees of consanguinity.
